title: The Death of Judas
sum: In spring 160 BC Demetrius sends Bacchides back to Judea with a large army. Judas has only three thousand men at Elasa, and most of them slip away until eight hundred are left. His men beg him to retreat, but he refuses: "Let us die with courage for our brothers' sake." He breaks the enemy's right wing but is caught from behind and killed. His brothers bury him at Modein, and all Israel mourns him in words taken from David's lament for Saul and Jonathan: "How the warrior has fallen, the one who saved Israel!"

With Judas gone, the renegades rule the country, famine sets in, and Israel's distress is the worst "since the day a prophet was last seen among them." Judas's friends choose his brother Jonathan as leader. He and Simon survive in the desert of Tekoa, avenge their brother John on the sons of Jambri, and escape Bacchides by swimming the Jordan. Bacchides rings Judea with forts and takes hostages; the high priest Alcimus starts to pull down a wall in the Temple court and is struck down. A second campaign fails at Bethbasi. Bacchides makes peace and leaves for good, and Jonathan settles at Michmash and "began to judge the people."
readings: A tragedy that is also a beginning

Read as a story, the chapter turns on one death. Judas chooses to fight when he cannot win, and the book honors the choice with the language of David's lament. But the chapter does not end in defeat: by 9:73 the land has rest and a new judge. The brothers' cause outlives its greatest fighter.

The chapter is full of echoes of Israel's early history: a rescuer mourned (Judges 3:9; 2 Samuel 1:19), the land quiet (Judges 3:11), a Jonathan at Michmash (1 Samuel 14), and a leader who "judges" the people (1 Samuel 7:15). The writer presents the Hasmonean brothers as the new judges God raised for Israel.

views.C: Western readers from Ambrose on have held up Judas's last stand as a model of courage. Ambrose of Milan, in his book on the duties of the clergy, praises Judas for choosing a glorious death over flight, citing his words at Elasa (in the Latin, "moriamur in virtute propter fratres nostros"), and sets him beside the martyrs of 2 Maccabees as an example of Christian fortitude.
views.H: Historians accept the outline: a defeat at Elasa in 160 BC, after which the movement survived as a guerrilla band. Many think the book's numbers (twenty-two thousand against eight hundred) inflate the odds to heighten the hero's death, and note that it says nothing of the treaty with Rome (chapter 8) bringing any help. The ring of forts (9:50–52) fits Seleucid practice.
views.J: The rabbis' stories of Hanukkah do not name Judas or tell of his death; the prayer Al ha-Nissim, said at Hanukkah, thanks God for the victories of "Mattathias son of Johanan, the high priest, the Hasmonean, and his sons." The Scroll of Antiochus (late antique or early medieval), read in some communities at Hanukkah, tells of Judas falling in battle, but rearranges the story so that his father Mattathias outlives him and leads the final victory.

deep.h: "How the warrior has fallen": Judas and David's lament
deep.b:
The lament in 9:21 is two lines, and both are borrowed. The first takes up David's refrain over Saul and Jonathan, "How the warriors have fallen!" (2 Samuel 1:19; 2 Samuel 1:25; 2 Samuel 1:27). The second calls Judas "the one who saved Israel", the role of the judges, whom the LORD raised up to rescue Israel (Judges 2:16); Othniel is "a rescuer" (Judges 3:9). The next verse copies the closing formula of the kings in the books of Kings: "The rest of Solomon's story ... is written in the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds" (1 Kings 11:41), except that Judas's story "was never written down, for there was a great deal of it" (9:22).

The borrowing does several things. It sets Judas beside Saul's son Jonathan, a brave warrior killed by foreigners, and it prepares for the next leader, who is also called Jonathan and settles at the first Jonathan's battlefield (9:73). It gives Judas the honor of a king without making him one; the Hasmoneans were not of David's line, and the book never claims they were. And it turns the defeat into a royal ending, the close of a reign. Readers who knew the Hebrew would also hear that the book's poetry here is not new verse but Scripture's own words reused, a habit of the writer throughout (compare 3:3–9; 14:4–15).

deep.h: Why does the book say no prophet was seen?
deep.b:
9:27 measures Israel's distress against the past: it was worse than any "since the day a prophet was last seen among them". With 4:46 and 14:41, it shows that the writer and his readers thought of their own time as one without prophets, waiting for one to come. Psalm 74:9 says the same. Josephus later says the exact line of prophets ended with Artaxerxes (Against Apion 1.41), and rabbinic tradition says that after the last prophets "the holy spirit departed from Israel" (Tosefta Sotah 13:3).

Readers have drawn different conclusions. Some Protestant writers have used the verse to argue that the book itself, written after prophecy ended, cannot be Scripture; Catholic and Orthodox writers answer that inspiration and prophecy are not the same thing, and that the verse is a historian's honesty, not a claim about the canon. That question is set out in a card on the book's opening page. Whether prophecy continues in the church is carded at Numbers 11.

echoes: 2 Samuel 1:19; 2 Samuel 1:25; 2 Samuel 1:27; Judges 2:16; Judges 3:9; Judges 3:11; 1 Kings 11:41; Psalm 74:9; Numbers 10:9; Deuteronomy 20:8; Joshua 7:6; Ezra 5:1–2; 1 Samuel 13:23; 1 Samuel 14:1–14; 1 Samuel 7:15; Amos 8:10

settings.what: Judas's last words to his men
settings.by: Judas, with the reply of his men (9:9)
settings.to: the eight hundred who stayed with him at Elasa
settings.when: spring 160 BC, as Bacchides' army of twenty thousand drew up for battle (9:3–6)
settings.why: To hold the last men together. His soldiers urge retreat; Judas refuses flight as a stain on their glory and accepts death "for our brothers' sake". The speech gives the reason the book honors a battle it lost.
settings.readers: The writer's first readers, Judeans under Simon's descendants, already knew how the day ended: they lived under the family of the brothers who survived it. The people's decree that the book quotes praises Simon and his brothers because they "put themselves in danger" for the sanctuary and the law (14:29); Judas's refusal to flee is the first and plainest case.

settings.by: "all Israel", in the words the writer gives them
settings.to: the dead Judas, and the people gathered to mourn him
settings.when: at his burial at Modein, after the defeat at Elasa (9:19)
settings.why: To mourn a fallen leader, and to give him a hero's honor in words taken from David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:19) and the judges' role as rescuers (Judges 3:9, "a rescuer").
settings.readers: The book was first written in Hebrew: Origen knew a Hebrew title for it, which Eusebius records (Church History 6.25.2), and Jerome says he found a Hebrew copy. Its first readers would have heard David's own Hebrew words in this lament, an echo the Greek translation keeps only in part.

settings.when: after Judas's death, in the famine and persecution of 160 BC (9:23–27)
settings.why: To find a new leader, since "there is no man like him". The choice is made by the faithful, not by any king, and it rests on Jonathan's family and the people's need.
settings.readers: The book's readers lived under Simon's descendants, whose right to rule rested on a similar public choice, the decree of 14:27–47. Many scholars think the writer told Jonathan's election this way to show the family's leadership as given by the people from the start.

settings.what: A report of the Jambri wedding
settings.when: some time after the sons of Jambri seized John and the baggage at Medeba (9:36)
settings.why: To tell the brothers where their brother's killers would be, and when they would be off guard. The report sets up the ambush and the brothers' revenge.
settings.readers: Medeba lay across the Jordan in Moab, beyond Judea's borders in Jonathan's day. By the time the book was written, John Hyrcanus had taken Medeba after a long siege, according to Josephus (Antiquities 13.255), so readers knew the town as a Hasmonean conquest.

settings.when: on a Sabbath, trapped between Bacchides' army and the Jordan (9:43)
settings.why: To brace the men for a fight with no way out, and to call them to prayer: "cry out to Heaven." It is the first speech of the new leader and shows him like Judas, fighting and praying.
settings.readers: The book never names God; it says "Heaven", as here, or nothing at all. The same reverent habit appears in Daniel (Daniel 4:26) and later in the rabbis' "kingdom of Heaven". The first readers, Hebrew-speaking Judeans, would have heard in Jonathan's "cry out to Heaven" their own way of praying.

settings.by: "all the lawless", Jews opposed to Jonathan
settings.when: after two years of peace, about 157 BC (9:57)
settings.why: To bring Bacchides back and destroy Jonathan's band while it felt safe. The plot fails, and its failure ends the war (9:60–72).
settings.readers: Readers under the later Hasmoneans had their own Jewish opponents. Josephus tells of a revolt against Alexander Jannaeus in which his opponents called in a Seleucid king, Demetrius III (Antiquities 13.376–379). Such readers could hear in "the lawless" who called in Bacchides the forerunners of their own enemies.

title: High Priest by Royal Letter
sum: In 152 BC a young claimant, Alexander Balas, seizes Ptolemais and declares himself king. Demetrius and Alexander now compete for Jonathan's support. Demetrius gives him the right to raise an army and frees the hostages, and Jonathan moves into Jerusalem and fortifies Mount Zion. Alexander answers with a greater gift: he appoints Jonathan high priest and Friend of the King, with a purple robe and a gold crown, and at the Feast of Booths Jonathan puts on the holy vestments. Demetrius replies with a letter to the whole nation promising tax relief, the Citadel, Ptolemais and much else, but the people do not trust him and stay with Alexander.

Alexander kills Demetrius in battle and marries Cleopatra, daughter of Ptolemy VI of Egypt, at Ptolemais. Jonathan attends the wedding; the king dresses him in purple, silences his accusers, and makes him general and governor. In 147 BC Demetrius's son lands from Crete, and his governor Apollonius taunts Jonathan to fight on the plain. Jonathan takes Joppa, beats Apollonius near Azotus, and burns the temple of Dagon with those who fled into it. Alexander rewards him with the gold brooch of the King's Kinsmen and the city of Ekron.
readings: The rise of the Hasmonean state

Read as history, the chapter shows how a guerrilla leader became a ruler. Jonathan wins little by battle and much by choosing sides: the high priesthood, royal titles and land come from kings who need his army. The book tells it as success, and many historians agree that it was.

Read beside the Torah and later Jewish debates, the chapter raises a question it never asks. The high priesthood, which the Law gives to Aaron's line and history had given to Zadok's, comes here from a Gentile king's letter, with purple and a crown. Some Jews of the time, very likely including the authors of some Dead Sea Scrolls, saw this as the corruption of the office.

views.C: Older Catholic scholarship, such as Bechtel's article in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), treated 1 Maccabees as trustworthy history, documents included.
views.H: Most historians accept the outline: Alexander's landing in 152 BC, Jonathan's appointment at Booths that year, Demetrius's death in 150 BC, the wedding at Ptolemais, and the battle near Azotus in 147 BC. Debate centers on the letters (10:25–45), whose generosity seems too great, and on Jonathan's priesthood, which many link with the "Wicked Priest" of the Dead Sea Scrolls.
views.J: Jewish memory of the Hasmonean priesthood is divided. The prayer Al ha-Nissim calls Mattathias "the high priest", while the Babylonian Talmud tells of a sage who told King Yannai to leave "the crown of priesthood to the seed of Aaron" (Kiddushin 66a), and Josephus gives a similar story of John Hyrcanus and the Pharisees (Antiquities 13.288–292).

deep.h: A high priest from a pagan king
deep.b:
By the Law, the high priest must come from Aaron's family (Exodus 28:1; Numbers 25:10–13), and from Solomon's time the family of Zadok held the office (1 Kings 2:35). That line was broken in the 170s BC, when Antiochus IV sold the office first to Jason and then to Menelaus, and Onias III was killed (2 Maccabees 4:7–34). Alcimus, though of Aaron's line, was appointed by Demetrius and is a villain in this book (7:5–25). After his death in 159 BC no high priest is named for seven years (9:56; Josephus, Antiquities 20.237). Then Jonathan, of the priestly course of Joarib (2:1; 1 Chronicles 24:7) but not of the high priestly house, receives the office by letter from Alexander Balas.

1 Maccabees tells this without apology. It sets the appointment among royal favors (purple, crown, the title Friend), and for the writer the family's deeds were enough. Later Jews were less sure. Josephus reports that the Pharisees asked John Hyrcanus to give up the high priesthood and be content to rule (Antiquities 13.288–292), and the Talmud tells a similar story of King Yannai (Kiddushin 66a).

The Wicked Priest. The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran describes a "Wicked Priest" who "was called by the name of truth when he first arose" but later grew proud, abandoned God for riches, and persecuted the community's Teacher of Righteousness (1QpHab 8:8–13; 11:4–8). Many scholars, among them Vermes, Milik, Stegemann and Murphy-O'Connor, identify him with Jonathan, who began as a zealous fighter, took the office from a Gentile king, and died in the hands of enemies (13:23). Stegemann suggested that the Teacher had himself served as high priest in the years after Alcimus. Cross preferred Simon; the Groningen hypothesis of García Martínez and van der Woude sees a series of Hasmonean high priests behind the title; others think of Alexander Jannaeus. The scrolls give no names, and the identification remains a theory. The topic Zadok gathers the evidence.

1 Maccabees quotes many official documents. In chapter 10 there are two royal letters to the Jews: Alexander's short letter to Jonathan (10:18–20) and Demetrius's long letter to the nation (10:25–45). The book also reports letters between Alexander and Ptolemy (10:51–56).

Reasons to think they rest on real documents. They use the forms and terms of Hellenistic royal letters: the greeting "to his brother ... greetings", the court titles, the technical words for taxes and exemptions. Demetrius writes to "the nation of the Jews" and never names Jonathan, which fits a king who would not recognize the high priest his rival had made; a writer inventing the letter would hardly have left the hero out. Josephus, who had access to other sources, retells both letters in detail (Antiquities 13.45–57).

Reasons for doubt. The Greek of the letters is the same translation-Greek as the rest of the book, so at most we have a translation of a translation. Demetrius's offers are extravagant: he gives up taxes on a scale no king could afford, and he gives the Temple Ptolemais, which his rival held. Some think the writer enlarged a real letter; others that he composed it to show how much the kings valued Jonathan.

Most historians, such as Schürer's revisers, Goldstein and Bartlett, take a middle view: the letters go back to real correspondence, edited and perhaps expanded by the writer. Bickerman's study of Seleucid administration found the terms used in the letters consistent with the period.

echoes: Exodus 28:1–4; Numbers 25:10–13; 1 Kings 2:35; 1 Chronicles 24:7; Leviticus 23:34; Genesis 41:42; Esther 6:7–11; Esther 8:15; 1 Samuel 5:2–5; 1 Kings 20:23; Daniel 11:17; Joshua 13:3; Hebrews 5:4

settings.by: King Demetrius I, with his reasoning given aloud (10:4–5)
settings.to: Jonathan, and through him the people and the men of the Citadel (10:7)
settings.when: 152 BC, just after Alexander Balas seized Ptolemais (10:1–2)
settings.why: To win Jonathan before Alexander could. The king grants him the right to raise troops and frees the hostages, a sign of how weak Demetrius's hold on Judea had become.
settings.readers: The writer gives the king's private motive, "he will remember all the harm we did", as if he knew the royal mind. Readers took such speeches as the historian's explanation, in the manner of Greek histories; Josephus, retelling it for Greek and Roman readers, kept the motive (Antiquities 13.37–42).

settings.when: 152 BC, after hearing of Demetrius's offers and Jonathan's record (10:15)
settings.why: To decide to outbid Demetrius. "Will we ever find another man like this?" is the writer's way of showing that the Gentile kings themselves recognized Jonathan's worth.
settings.readers: For Hasmonean-era readers, praise from a king was proof of standing; the same pattern recurs when Rome and Sparta honor the family (chapters 8, 12 and 14). The book has no copy among the Dead Sea Scrolls, whose authors, if they meant Jonathan by the Wicked Priest, would have read his royal favor very differently.

settings.what: Alexander's letter appointing Jonathan high priest
settings.when: 152 BC, before the Feast of Booths (10:21)
settings.why: To bind Jonathan to Alexander's side by the highest honor in Judea, the high priesthood, with the court rank of Friend and the purple and crown.
settings.readers: Jews who opposed the Hasmonean priesthood, as many did by the book's own time, could point to this letter: the office came from a Gentile pretender. The writer quotes it anyway, which suggests that his readers accepted royal appointment as normal, as it had been for every high priest since Jason.
views: Most historians think it rests on a real document, since its form is that of Hellenistic royal letters and it matches what is known of Alexander's need for allies.
Some think the writer reshaped it to stress Jonathan's worth (10:19), as he often frames documents with his own comments.

settings.when: 152 BC, on hearing of Jonathan's appointment
settings.why: To show the bidding war from the losing side. Demetrius admits he has been outplayed and resolves to offer more.
settings.readers: The first readers, under John Hyrcanus or his sons, knew that Seleucid kings were not always this weak: in Hyrcanus's first year Antiochus VII besieged Jerusalem and broke down its walls (Josephus, Antiquities 13.236–248). A king admitting he had been outplayed by the Jews was a memory worth keeping.

settings.what: Demetrius's long letter to the nation
settings.to: "the nation of the Jews", not Jonathan by name
settings.when: 152 BC, after Alexander's letter (10:18–20)
settings.why: To win the people over their new high priest's head: freedom from tribute, salt tax, crown taxes and crop shares; the Citadel; three districts from Samaria; Ptolemais for the Temple; Jewish troops in royal service; asylum at the Temple; and money for the sanctuary and the walls.
settings.readers: The list is a rare view of what Seleucid rule cost Judea, and readers in the book's own time would know which promises were later kept: tribute relief came under Demetrius II (11:28; 13:36–40), and the Citadel fell only to Simon (13:49–52). The people's refusal (10:46) tells them the writer's lesson: promises from such kings are not to be trusted.
views: Most historians accept a real document behind it, pointing to the technical terms and to the address to the nation rather than to Jonathan.
Others think the writer expanded or wrote it, pointing to its huge concessions and the gift of Ptolemais, which Demetrius did not hold.

settings.to: Ptolemy VI Philometor, king of Egypt
settings.when: 150 BC, after the death of Demetrius I (10:50)
settings.why: To claim victory and ask for Ptolemy's daughter in marriage, sealing the alliance with Egypt.
settings.readers: Readers knew the outcome: within five years Ptolemy took the bride back and turned against Alexander (11:9–12). Those who knew Daniel 11, written a generation before the book, would recognize the pattern of marriages between the kings of north and south that fail (Daniel 11:6; Daniel 11:17).

settings.when: 150 BC
settings.why: To accept the marriage and fix the place, Ptolemais. The friendly words prepare for the betrayal in 11:1, which the book blames on Ptolemy's trickery.
settings.readers: Judean readers knew Ptolemy VI as the king who let Onias IV build a rival temple at Leontopolis (Josephus, Antiquities 13.62–73), and the book gives him no credit. If the Greek translation was read among Egypt's Jews, whose leaders Onias and Dositheus had commanded this king's army (Josephus, Against Apion 2.49), the harsh picture of him in 11:1–11 would have read differently there.

settings.what: The king's order to the herald
settings.to: his officers, to be proclaimed in Ptolemais
settings.when: 150 BC, at the royal wedding (10:57–62)
settings.why: To protect Jonathan publicly: no one may bring charges against him. It silences his Jewish accusers (10:61, 64).
settings.readers: The scene follows the pattern of Joseph and Mordecai, Jews robed and proclaimed by a foreign king while their enemies are shamed (Genesis 41:42; Esther 6:11). Its first readers lived under rulers whose purple was by then their own privilege: the decree for Simon forbids anyone else in the country to wear purple or a gold clasp (14:44).

settings.by: Apollonius, governor of Coele-Syria, for Demetrius II
settings.when: 147 BC, after Demetrius II landed (10:67–69)
settings.why: To provoke Jonathan into fighting on the coastal plain, where cavalry would give Apollonius the advantage. The taunt recalls Israel's old defeats in its own land.
settings.readers: The taunt sounds like Goliath's (1 Samuel 17:44) and the Arameans' claim that Israel's "god is a god of the mountains" (1 Kings 20:23), and readers who knew those stories expected the boaster to lose. In the book's own day the coastal cities Apollonius speaks for were still independent; Alexander Jannaeus conquered most of them, Gaza among them, a generation or two later (Josephus, Antiquities 13.356–364).

title: Kings Rise and Fall
sum: Ptolemy VI marches north with a great army, putting garrisons in the coastal towns. Jonathan meets him with honor at Joppa and escorts him to the Eleutherus River. Ptolemy turns against his son-in-law Alexander, gives Cleopatra to Demetrius II, and enters Antioch wearing the crowns of Asia and Egypt. Alexander is beaten and flees to Arabia, where Zabdiel cuts off his head; Ptolemy dies three days later, and Demetrius II becomes king in 145 BC. Jonathan besieges the Citadel, goes boldly to the angry king at Ptolemais, and wins confirmation as high priest, freedom from tribute and three districts from Samaria.

Demetrius dismisses his father's troops, and Tryphon, Alexander's former officer, plots to crown Alexander's young son. When Antioch rises against Demetrius, three thousand Jewish soldiers save him and burn the city. But Demetrius breaks his promises, and Jonathan goes over to the boy king Antiochus VI, who confirms him as high priest and makes Simon governor of the coast. Jonathan campaigns from Ascalon to Damascus. Ambushed near Hazor by Demetrius's generals, his army flees; he tears his clothes, prays, turns the battle and returns to Jerusalem.
readings: Read politically, chapter 11 shows three changes of king in a few years and Jonathan gaining at every turn. The book's comment is in 11:53: kings lie. Loyalty goes to whoever keeps faith, and the Jews' strength lies in their own army.

Read religiously, the chapter ends as many stories in Judges and Joshua do: defeat, grief, prayer and a sudden turn (11:69–72). The writer does not name God, but the shape of the story points to Heaven's help, and the battle near Hazor recalls Joshua's (Joshua 11).

views.H: Historians check this chapter against Josephus, Diodorus, Polybius and Strabo. The main events are confirmed: Ptolemy VI's march, the fall of Alexander Balas, Ptolemy's death in 145 BC, the riot at Antioch and the rise of Tryphon. The book differs on details: it makes Ptolemy a schemer from the start. Josephus agrees that he put on both diadems but says he soon gave Syria up to Demetrius for fear of Rome (Antiquities 13.113–115), and Diodorus says he declined it (32.9c). Its numbers at Antioch are exaggerated.
views.J: Josephus, retelling the chapter for Greek and Roman readers, tells it in Ptolemy's favor, adding a plot by Alexander's minister Ammonius against him and Ptolemy's quick surrender of the Syrian throne (Antiquities 13.103–115). He keeps the Jewish rescue of Demetrius at Antioch and its glory for the Jews (13.135–142).
views.P: Protestant readers have long valued these chapters as history while denying them the authority of Scripture. Luther's preface of 1533 says 1 Maccabees is close to the other books of Scripture in its language and worth reading, especially to understand Daniel 11, where the wars between the kings of north and south are foretold.

deep.h: The Seleucid civil wars and Jonathan's alliances
deep.b:
From 152 BC the Seleucid kingdom had two or more kings at a time. Alexander Balas, backed by Rome, Pergamum and Egypt, killed Demetrius I in 150 BC. In 147 BC Demetrius II landed from Crete. In 145 BC Ptolemy VI changed sides, Alexander was killed, and Ptolemy died of his wounds, leaving Demetrius II king. Within a year, Tryphon raised Alexander's son as Antiochus VI and took Antioch. Later still (in chapters 12–13) Tryphon killed both the boy and Jonathan.

Jonathan's course through these years was consistent: support whoever would give the most and could be trusted. He stayed with Alexander to the end (10:47), escorted Ptolemy without fighting him (11:6–7), won Demetrius II by gifts and courage (11:23–27), saved him at Antioch (11:44–51), and left him when he broke his word (11:53–57). Each change brought Judea more: the high priesthood confirmed, tax freedom, new districts, and for Simon command of the coast. Historians see the method as the main reason the Hasmoneans gained independence; the book presents it as loyalty betrayed by faithless kings.

echoes: Joshua 11:1–11; Joshua 11:4; Joshua 7:6; Judges 4:2–6; Judges 7:12; Daniel 11:6; Daniel 11:17; Psalm 146:3; Genesis 45:8; Luke 5:1; Ezra 4:10–11; Joshua 20:7; Esther 1:7

settings.when: about 146–145 BC, after Ptolemy had taken the coastal towns (11:8)
settings.why: To change sides: Ptolemy offers Demetrius his daughter and the throne, and accuses Alexander of trying to kill him. The book adds that he spoke ill of Alexander because he wanted his kingdom (11:11).
settings.readers: The writer tells his Judean readers how to hear these words: Ptolemy "spoke ill of him because he wanted his kingdom" (11:11). That judgment is the writer's own. Josephus, who also used non-Jewish histories, reports a real plot against Ptolemy by Alexander's minister Ammonius (Antiquities 13.106–108), so the first readers were given one side of a disputed story.

settings.when: 145 BC, after renegades reported the siege of the Citadel (11:20–21)
settings.why: To stop the siege and bring Jonathan to account at Ptolemais. Jonathan's answer, to keep the siege going and come in person with gifts, shows his nerve.
settings.readers: The Citadel stood in Jerusalem until 141 BC (13:49–52), so the book's readers knew how long this siege lasted. Simon's capture of it was celebrated each year in the Hasmonean calendar, and later appears in the list of feast days in Megillat Taanit.

settings.what: Demetrius II's letter, with his letter to Lasthenes
settings.to: "his brother Jonathan and the nation of the Jews", enclosing a copy of his orders to Lasthenes
settings.when: 145 BC, after Jonathan won the king's favor at Ptolemais (11:24–29)
settings.why: To grant what Jonathan asked: freedom from royal dues, the three districts of Aphairema, Lydda and Rathamin, and the tithes, tolls, salt pans and crowns. The letter is to be copied and set up on the holy mountain.
settings.readers: Unlike Demetrius I's letter, this one is addressed to Jonathan by name and fits the request of 11:28, so most historians trust it more. Readers in Jerusalem could, the writer implies, see a copy set up on the Temple mount (11:37); none survives. Josephus gives a version of it (Antiquities 13.126–128).
views: Most historians accept it as a real document: it is modest, specific and fits later events (13:36–40).
A few think its wording was adjusted, since its terms overlap so closely with Demetrius I's promises in 10:29–31.

settings.when: about 145 BC, as his army turned against him (11:38–40)
settings.why: To get soldiers: the king promises great honor in return for men to defend him. The promise prepares for its breaking in 11:53.
settings.readers: For the first readers the story of a Seleucid king begging Jewish troops for help was a reversal of chapter 1, where the king's army had crushed Jerusalem. By their time the roles had shifted further: John Hyrcanus, Josephus says, was the first Jewish ruler to keep foreign mercenaries of his own (Antiquities 13.249).

settings.what: The people of Antioch beg for peace
settings.when: about 145 BC, after the Jewish troops had burned part of the city (11:47–48)
settings.why: To surrender on terms: they ask for "right hands", a pledge of safety, and for the Jews to stop fighting.
settings.readers: Judean readers heard this as the high point of Jewish arms abroad: the Seleucid capital, which had sent armies against Jerusalem, now begged the king to stop the Jews. Josephus kept the episode in full (Antiquities 13.133–142).

settings.by: the young King Antiochus VI, for Tryphon
settings.when: about 144 BC, after Tryphon took Antioch (11:54–56)
settings.why: To win Jonathan from Demetrius by confirming his high priesthood, adding a fourth district and making him a Friend of the King, with Simon as governor of the coast (11:59).
settings.readers: Readers knew that the boy king and Jonathan would both die at Tryphon's hands (12:48; 13:23; 13:31). The letter's honors, read with that end in mind, show how little a king's grant was worth, the same lesson the book draws in 11:53.

settings.to: God, though the words are not given and God is not named
settings.when: about 144 BC, near Hazor, when all but two of his officers had fled (11:69–70)
settings.why: To turn to God in disaster. Torn clothes and dust on the head are the signs of grief and repentance; the prayer is followed at once by victory (11:72).
settings.readers: The first readers knew this gesture from Joshua 7:6 and from the book's own scenes of public mourning, at Mizpah and before the ruined Temple (3:47; 4:39). The writer gives no words of the prayer: as throughout, the turn of the battle that follows (11:72) is left to show who answered it.
